blocks.text: Verses 1-6 are often grouped with Jeremiah’s first-person laments, sometimes called his “confessions.” Such passages give voice to accusation, isolation, protest, compulsion, petition, and despair. That label can help readers notice the unusually direct argument in these verses: the speaker affirms God’s righteousness while asking why treacherous people prosper and then brings his own vulnerability before God. The exact boundaries of these laments and how directly they reflect biography remain disputed.

Jeremiah belongs to a book that brings together poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix. A practical outline places chapter 12 within chapters 2-25, without settling how the book was composed. This larger variety helps explain why a concentrated first-person protest can stand within a book containing several different literary forms.
